> It may be better to use `ICollection<>`

That's correct, but I don't like the cost of making a virtual call over the interface, as the performance is critical here.

> would it make sense to add array-like methods?

No, I don't think so. The point here is to make the return value meaningful, and I don't see how introducing an array-like indexer helps with that.

> Seeing as these non-allocating APIs have different signatures, would it make sense to implement them on the C++ side so they are exposed to GDScript?

No, the word `Non-Allocating` here refers to `Not Allocate GC-tracked objects`, which is not present in the GDScript world.

> Should those methods even return dictionaries in the first place?

No, they shouldn't, and that's exactly why proper `struct` support for Godot is currently on the drawing board, which isn't available yet.

> Is `{Method}NonAlloc` the best name for these APIs? It's used by Unity but it feels clunky.

It may not be the best name, but it conveys the intention well, and it's not patented, so I'm using it for now. Consider it temporary.

> Maybe it should be an overload of the original method?

It won't work for places where the return value only differs.

> maxResults is ambiguous in IntersectPointNonAlloc if the list already contains elements.

This method is meant for advanced users, and it's better to leave the sanitation to them, as [clearing a List of managed-type-containing-structs also has extra overhead](https://source.dot.net/#System.Private.CoreLib/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/List.cs,329).

> An alternative approach could be to have a specialised struct-based list type that doesn't allocate when the number of elements is low.

This simple use case doesn't require a dedicated struct type. The `ValueCollection` needs to be specifically disposed of (`using` or `Dispose`) to prevent managed memory leaks (we don't have deconstructors as a fail-safe for structs). Also, renting and returning from the array pool have overheads (slot selection, zeroing), which I'm unwilling to take.

But with that said, if we eventually migrate to .NET 10, we might benefit from the new de-abstraction optimization, as JIT or ILC may recognize that we are always using certain types over that interface.

e.g.:
```csharp
public static void Main(string[] args)
{
    List<float> list = [];
    HashSet<float> hashSet = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++)
    {
        InterfaceMethod(list);
        InterfaceMethod(hashSet);
        list.Clear();
        hashSet.Clear();
    }
    Console.WriteLine(list.Count);
    Console.WriteLine(hashSet.Count);
}


[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]
static void InterfaceMethod(ICollection<float> collection)
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
    {
        collection.Add(i * 0.5f);
    }
}
```

I am thinking - would it make sense to accept a span instead of a list for results?

For example, change this:
```cs
public unsafe void CollideShapeNonAlloc(PhysicsShapeQueryParameters3D parameters, List<Vector3> results, int maxResults = 32)
```

Into this:
```cs
public unsafe int CollideShapeNonAlloc(PhysicsShapeQueryParameters3D parameters, Span<Vector3> results)
```

That way, there would be no risk of growing a list (and reducing performance) during an `Add` operation. It would also work for arrays, lists, and stackalloc spans.

I made this quick benchmark to demonstrate the difference between re-using a node, doing a raycast on the DirectSpaceState, and using the new non-allocating raycast on the DirectSpaceState. [NonAllocPerf.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30557898/NonAllocPerf.zip) There's 5 options: `Collide `will determine if the next test will collide with a CSGBox `Benchmark Node` will test the performance of re-using an already instantiated Raycast3D Node over and over by calling `ForceRaycastUpdate` `Benchmark Raycast` will test the performance using the normal DSS raycast which returns a GodotDictionary `Benchmark Non-Alloc Raycast` will test the performance of using the new Non-Allocating method `Number of Rays` determines how many rays will be fired ______ Here are the results of a test where Collision is disabled: ____ Here are the results of a test where Collision is enabled: ____ It sort of surprised me just how poorly the normal allocating method does, there's basically no reason to ever use this method as far as I can tell? Though the more interesting thing is that the Node based raycast seems to have better efficiency when colliding with something compared to the non-allocating method. I've tested to make sure this isn't because of assigning data to the structs and the results are the same. It seems like, on average at least, re-using a Raycast Node ends up winning out, as the difference in colliding with something is far greater than the difference in not colliding. Though, of course, if your game has more raycasts that don't collide more than they do, then the non-allocating method wins out. I am wondering if there's anything to be done so that the non-allocating method _always_ wins out? I am weary of using this PR for the AI generation concerns, but I was curious about how it would do, and maybe these results could help you in thinking how to rewrite it?

> I am wondering if there's anything to be done so that the non-allocating method always wins out?
> I am weary of using this PR for the AI generation concerns, but I was curious about how it would do, and maybe these results could help you in thinking how to rewrite it?

Thanks, I will certainly look into it this week. I guess the Node-based algorithm generally has less overhead (on the engine side), and their is less we have do on the interop layer side, but I would certainly bench them carefully.

Re-ran the Intersect3D benchmark, I think I may have accidentally gave incorrect information regarding performance, after seeing very very peculiar results with running 1 ray, it popped into my mind that the editor may be messing with the results. I'm not really sure why I trusted editor based tests to begin with and that's my fault, here are the updated results when actually running the game (Tested during _Ready, but fired some rays prior to warm-up beloved JIT): It seems like, the non-alloc method actually does win out against the Raycast3D node in basically every scenario. I'm unsure if this is because of the recent changes, but given the results I was getting in the editor were identical to the results to the prior commit, it's likely my test was just poorly done. The poor allocating method still gets destroyed by both methods, which makes me think the release this is included in should note that people should move to the non-allocating method? It's current state seems like a footgun (especially with it being a GodotDictionary) and I fear a "NonAlloc" method may sound "technical" and push people away from trying what is really an objectively better way. If someone with a bit more expertise in benchmarking these kind of things in C# could create a test to double check my work I would be grateful, these values feel a bit more sane to me, but I'm not sure I trust myself.
